problems.html: For f(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2}f(x)=x2, find the equations of the tangent and the normal to the curve at the point (2,4)(2,4)(2,4).
hints: The tangent's slope at a point is the derivative evaluated there; the normal is perpendicular to it.
Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1-1−1, so the normal's slope is −1/f′(2)-1/f'(2)−1/f′(2).
Use point–slope form y−y0=m(x−x0)y-y_0=m(x-x_0)y−y0​=m(x−x0​) for each line, with the same point (2,4)(2,4)(2,4) but the two different slopes.
problems.format: tangent slope, intercept; then the normal's

problems.html: Evaluate, stating that the form is indeterminate before applying the rule: (a) lim⁡x→0sin⁡xx,(b) lim⁡x→0ex−1x,(c) lim⁡x→∞ln⁡xx2.\text{(a)}\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^{x}-1}{x},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln x}{x^{2}} .(a) x→0lim​xsinx​,(b) x→0lim​xex−1​,(c) x→∞lim​x2lnx​.
hints: Check the form first: l'Hôpital applies only to 00\tfrac0000​ and ∞∞\tfrac{\infty}{\infty}∞∞​, so confirm you have one before differentiating.
Then differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately — this is not the quotient rule, and mixing the two up is the standard error.
In (c) the form is ∞∞\tfrac{\infty}{\infty}∞∞​; after one application you get 1/x2x\dfrac{1/x}{2x}2x1/x​, which simplifies before you take the limit.
problems.format: (a), (b), (c) — comma-separated

problems.html: Locate and classify the stationary points of f(x)=x3−3x2f(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}f(x)=x3−3x2 using the second-derivative test.
hints: Stationary points are where f′f'f′ vanishes, so differentiate and factorise rather than expanding.
The second-derivative test then classifies each: negative means a local maximum, positive a local minimum.
Remember to compute the yyy-coordinate of each point by substituting back into fff, not into f′f'f′.
problems.format: the local max point; then the local min

problems.html: Find the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of (a) f(x)=1x−2,(b) g(x)=2xx−3.\text{(a)}\ f(x)=\frac{1}{x-2},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ g(x)=\frac{2x}{x-3} .(a) f(x)=x−21​,(b) g(x)=x−32x​.
hints: A vertical asymptote sits where the denominator vanishes and the numerator does not.
A horizontal asymptote comes from the behaviour as x→±∞x\to\pm\inftyx→±∞, so divide top and bottom by the highest power of xxx.
In (a) the numerator is constant, so the quotient dies away to zero; in (b) both are degree one, so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients.
problems.format: (a) then (b): vertical, horizontal

problems.html: Two non-negative numbers add to 101010. What is the largest their product can be?
hints: Name the two numbers so that the constraint is already built in: if one is xxx, the other is forced.
That turns the product into a function of one variable on a closed interval, which you can then maximise.
Differentiate, solve for the stationary point, and confirm with the second derivative — then check the endpoints too, since they are part of the domain.
problems.format: the largest possible product

problems.html: Apply gradient descent to f(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2}f(x)=x2 with learning rate η=0.1\eta=0.1η=0.1, starting from x0=1x_{0}=1x0​=1. Compute x1x_{1}x1​ and x2x_{2}x2​, and state the limit of the iteration.
hints: The update rule is xn+1=xn−ηf′(xn)x_{n+1}=x_n-\eta f'(x_n)xn+1​=xn​−ηf′(xn​), so work out f′f'f′ first and substitute the given η\etaη.
Here that simplifies to a single multiplication: xn+1=0.8 xnx_{n+1}=0.8\,x_nxn+1​=0.8xn​.
Iterating a constant multiplier gives a geometric sequence, so the limit is decided entirely by whether that multiplier is smaller than 111 in size.
problems.format: x₁, x₂, then the limit

problems.html: Show that f(x)=x2/3f(x)=x^{2/3}f(x)=x2/3 has a critical point at x=0x=0x=0 even though f′(0)f'(0)f′(0) does not exist, and decide whether it is a local maximum or minimum.
hints: A critical point is one where f′f'f′ is either zero or else fails to exist, provided the point is in the domain — the second case is what this problem is about.
Differentiate for x≠0x\neq0x=0 and see what happens to 23x−1/3\tfrac23x^{-1/3}32​x−1/3 as xxx approaches zero.
The second-derivative test cannot be used, since f′′f''f′′ does not exist there either. Use the first-derivative test: check the sign of f′f'f′ on each side.
problems.format: maximum or minimum at x = 0

problems.html: Show that x3+x−1=0x^{3}+x-1=0x3+x−1=0 has a solution in the interval (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).
hints: The intermediate value theorem needs two things: a continuous function, and two points where it takes opposite signs.
Polynomials are continuous everywhere, so only the sign change has to be checked.
Evaluate the function at each endpoint of the interval; if the values straddle zero, a root lies between them.
problems.format: f(0) and f(1) — comma-separated

problems.html: Let f(x)=x5+x+1f(x)=x^{5}+x+1f(x)=x5+x+1. Given that fff is one-to-one, find (f−1)′(1)\bigl(f^{-1}\bigr)'(1)(f−1)′(1) without finding f−1f^{-1}f−1 explicitly.
hints: The rule is (f−1)′(b)=1f′(a)\bigl(f^{-1}\bigr)'(b)=\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}(f−1)′(b)=f′(a)1​, where aaa is the point with f(a)=bf(a)=bf(a)=b.
So the first job is to find aaa with f(a)=1f(a)=1f(a)=1 — try small whole numbers rather than solving the quintic.
Then differentiate fff, evaluate at that aaa, and take the reciprocal. The inverse function itself is never needed.
problems.format: the value of (f⁻¹)′(1)

problems.html: Sketch the parabola f(x)=x2−4x+3f(x)=x^{2}-4x+3f(x)=x2−4x+3 by first using its derivative: find the interval(s) of increase and decrease and the vertex, then add the intercepts.
hints: Differentiate first: the sign of f′f'f′ tells you where the curve falls and where it rises, and the changeover is the vertex.
f′(x)=2x−4f'(x)=2x-4f′(x)=2x−4 is negative to the left of x=2x=2x=2 and positive to the right, so the vertex sits there.
For the intercepts, factorise the quadratic for the xxx-axis crossings and set x=0x=0x=0 for the yyy-axis one.
problems.format: vertex; x-intercepts; then the y-intercept

problems.html: Find the value of ccc guaranteed by the mean value theorem for f(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2}f(x)=x2 on [1,3][1,3][1,3].
hints: Check the hypotheses first: continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open one.
The theorem promises a ccc where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope f(b)−f(a)b−a\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}b−af(b)−f(a)​.
Compute that average slope as a number, set f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) equal to it, and solve — then confirm the answer lies strictly inside the interval.
problems.format: the value of c

problems.html: Use the closed-interval (extreme-value-theorem) method to find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x)=x2−4x+1f(x)=x^{2}-4x+1f(x)=x2−4x+1 on [0,3][0,3][0,3].
hints: On a closed bounded interval the extremes occur either at an interior critical point or at an endpoint — so find all the candidates first.
Solve f′(x)=0f'(x)=0f′(x)=0 and keep only the solutions lying inside [0,3][0,3][0,3].
Then simply compare the values of fff at that critical point and at both endpoints. No classification test is needed: the largest and smallest values win.
problems.format: max value and where; then min value and where

problems.html:
Consider the curve y=x3−2x+1y=x^{3}-2x+1y=x3−2x+1.

  1. Find the tangent and normal lines at the point where x=1x=1x=1.

  2. Find the equations of all tangent lines to the curve that are parallel to the line y=xy=xy=x.
hints: For (a) the recipe is unchanged: evaluate fff and f′f'f′ at the point, then use point–slope form twice.
For (b), 'parallel to y=xy=xy=x' means the slope is 111, so solve f′(x)=1f'(x)=1f′(x)=1 — a quadratic, so expect two points, not one.
Find the yyy-coordinate at each solution and write down both tangent lines; one of them you have already met in part (a).
problems.format: the two y-intercepts in (b), increasing

problems.html: Evaluate, first rewriting each into a 00\tfrac0000​ or ∞∞\tfrac{\infty}{\infty}∞∞​ form where necessary: (a) lim⁡x→0x−sin⁡xx3,(b) lim⁡x→0+xln⁡x,(c) lim⁡x→0 ⁣(1x−1sin⁡x).\text{(a)}\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{x-\sin x}{x^{3}},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \lim_{x\to0^{+}} x\ln x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \lim_{x\to0}\!\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{\sin x}\right).(a) x→0lim​x3x−sinx​,(b) x→0+lim​xlnx,(c) x→0lim​(x1​−sinx1​).
hints: Only (a) is already in a form l'Hôpital accepts; (b) and (c) must be rewritten into 00\tfrac0000​ or ∞∞\tfrac{\infty}{\infty}∞∞​ first.
For (b), a 0⋅∞0\cdot\infty0⋅∞ product becomes a quotient by putting one factor into the denominator: write xln⁡xx\ln xxlnx as ln⁡x1/x\dfrac{\ln x}{1/x}1/xlnx​.

For (c), an ∞−∞\infty-\infty∞−∞ difference becomes a quotient by combining over a common denominator. And in (a), check the form is still indeterminate before each new application — you will need three.
problems.format: (a), (b), (c) — comma-separated

problems.html: Locate and classify all stationary points of f(x)=2x3−3x2−12x+5.f(x)=2x^{3}-3x^{2}-12x+5 .f(x)=2x3−3x2−12x+5.
hints: Differentiate and factorise; the quadratic 6x2−6x−126x^2-6x-126x2−6x−12 has a common factor worth taking out first.
Apply the second-derivative test at each stationary point: the sign of f′′f''f′′ decides the type.
Substitute each stationary xxx back into the original cubic — not into f′f'f′ — to get the coordinates.
problems.format: the local max point; then the local min

problems.html: Carry out a full curve-sketching analysis of f(x)=x3−6x2+9xf(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9xf(x)=x3−6x2+9x (domain/symmetry, intercepts, increase/decrease and extrema, concavity and inflection) and sketch the curve.
hints: Work through the checklist in order: intercepts, then f′f'f′ for increase and decrease, then f′′f''f′′ for concavity.
The cubic factorises as x(x−3)2x(x-3)^2x(x−3)2, which tells you the intercepts and warns that the curve touches the axis at the repeated root rather than crossing it.
An inflection point needs f′′f''f′′ to change sign, not merely to vanish; here f′′f''f′′ is linear, so it changes sign at its single zero.
problems.format: the max point; the min point; the inflection

problems.html: Sketch f(x)=x2+1x2−1f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}+1}{x^{2}-1}f(x)=x2−1x2+1​: state the domain, symmetry, intercepts, asymptotes, stationary points and concavity, then draw the curve.
hints: Start with the domain: the denominator vanishes at two points, and each gives a vertical asymptote.
Check symmetry before doing any work — the function depends on xxx only through x2x^2x2, which halves the effort.
Use the quotient rule for f′f'f′; the numerator collapses dramatically, leaving a single stationary point, at x=0x=0x=0.
problems.format: the local max point; then the horizontal asymptote's y

problems.html: An open-topped box is made from a square sheet of card of side 12 cm12\,\text{cm}12cm by cutting a small square of side xxx from each corner and folding up the flaps. Find the value of xxx that maximises the volume, and the maximum volume.
hints: Express the box's dimensions in terms of the cut xxx: the height is xxx and the base is a square whose side has lost xxx from each end.
That gives V(x)=x(12−2x)2V(x)=x(12-2x)^2V(x)=x(12−2x)2 on the interval where all dimensions stay positive — state that interval, since it rules out a spurious root later.
Differentiate with the product rule and take out the common factor (12−2x)(12-2x)(12−2x); one of the two resulting roots lies outside the legal range.
problems.format: x in cm, then the maximum volume in cm³

problems.html: A battery of EMF ε\varepsilonε and internal resistance rrr delivers power P(R)=ε2R(R+r)2P(R)=\dfrac{\varepsilon^{2}R}{(R+r)^{2}}P(R)=(R+r)2ε2R​ to an external load of resistance R>0R>0R>0. Show that the power delivered is greatest when R=rR=rR=r, and find that maximum power.
hints: Treat ε\varepsilonε and rrr as constants and differentiate with respect to RRR alone — the quotient rule applies as usual.
The factor (R+r)(R+r)(R+r) is common to both terms of the numerator, so cancel one power of it before simplifying.
You should reach P′(R)=ε2r−R(R+r)3P'(R)=\varepsilon^2\dfrac{r-R}{(R+r)^3}P′(R)=ε2(R+r)3r−R​. The denominator is positive for R>0R>0R>0, so the sign of P′P'P′ is decided entirely by r−Rr-Rr−R.
problems.format: the k in P_max = ε²/(k r)

problems.html: A projectile is launched from level ground with fixed speed vvv at an angle θ\thetaθ to the horizontal. Neglecting air resistance, its range is R(θ)=v2g sin⁡(2θ),0≤θ≤π2.R(\theta)=\frac{v^{2}}{g}\,\sin(2\theta),\qquad\allowbreak 0\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}.R(θ)=gv2​sin(2θ),0≤θ≤2π​. Find the launch angle that maximises the range, and the maximum range.
hints: Only θ\thetaθ varies; vvv and ggg are constants that come along for the ride.
Differentiating sin⁡(2θ)\sin(2\theta)sin(2θ) needs the chain rule, so a factor of 222 appears.
Solve cos⁡(2θ)=0\cos(2\theta)=0cos(2θ)=0 within the stated range, then confirm it is a maximum — and note that both endpoints give zero range, which is a useful sanity check.
problems.format: the optimal launch angle in degrees

problems.html:
Given data values x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n}x1​,…,xn​, the sum of squared errors of a single predicted constant ccc is L(c)=∑i=1n(xi−c)2L(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}-c)^{2}L(c)=∑i=1n​(xi​−c)2.

  1. Show that LLL is minimised when ccc equals the mean xˉ=1n∑ixi\bar x=\tfrac1n\sum_i x_ixˉ=n1​∑i​xi​.

  2. Find the minimising ccc for the data {2,4,9}\{2,4,9\}{2,4,9}.
hints: Differentiate the sum with respect to ccc, remembering that each term contributes by the chain rule and that the xix_ixi​ are constants.
The sum splits: ∑2(xi−c)(−1)=2(nc−∑xi)\sum 2(x_i-c)(-1)=2\bigl(nc-\sum x_i\bigr)∑2(xi​−c)(−1)=2(nc−∑xi​). Setting that to zero gives ccc directly.
Check with the second derivative, which is 2n>02n>02n>0 and so independent of ccc — the minimum is unique. Then just average the three numbers.
problems.format: the minimising c for {2,4,9}

problems.html:
Minimise f(x)=x2−4x+5f(x)=x^{2}-4x+5f(x)=x2−4x+5 by gradient descent with learning rate η=0.25\eta=0.25η=0.25, starting from x0=0x_{0}=0x0​=0.

  1. Write the update rule xn+1=g(xn)x_{n+1}=g(x_n)xn+1​=g(xn​) explicitly and compute x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}x1​,x2​,x3​.

  2. To what value do the iterates converge, and why is that the right answer?

  3. What would go wrong if the learning rate were taken as η=1.5\eta=1.5η=1.5?
hints: Compute f′f'f′ first, then substitute into xn+1=xn−ηf′(xn)x_{n+1}=x_n-\eta f'(x_n)xn+1​=xn​−ηf′(xn​) and simplify to a single linear map.
You should reach xn+1=0.5xn+1x_{n+1}=0.5x_n+1xn+1​=0.5xn​+1; now iterate it three times from x0=0x_0=0x0​=0.

The limit is the fixed point, found by solving x=0.5x+1x=0.5x+1x=0.5x+1. For (c), redo the algebra with η=1.5\eta=1.5η=1.5 and look at the multiplier in front of xnx_nxn​ — its size decides everything.
problems.format: x₁, x₂, x₃, then the limit

problems.html:
1. Find the value of ccc guaranteed by the mean value theorem for f(x)=x3f(x)=x^{3}f(x)=x3 on [0,2][0,2][0,2].

  2. Use the mean value theorem to prove that ∣sin⁡a−sin⁡b∣≤∣a−b∣\left|\sin a-\sin b\right|\le\left|a-b\right|∣sina−sinb∣≤∣a−b∣ for all real a,ba,ba,b.
hints: For (a), set f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) equal to the average slope across the interval and solve for ccc.

For (b), apply the mean value theorem to sin⁡\sinsin on the interval with endpoints aaa and bbb: it gives sin⁡a−sin⁡b=cos⁡(c)(a−b)\sin a-\sin b=\cos(c)(a-b)sina−sinb=cos(c)(a−b) for some ccc between them.
Now take absolute values and use the one fact you know about every cosine: it never exceeds 111 in size.
problems.format: the value of c in (a), to 3 d.p.

problems.html:
Let f(x)=2x+cos⁡xf(x)=2x+\cos xf(x)=2x+cosx.

  1. Show that fff is strictly increasing on R\mathbb{R}R, hence one-to-one and invertible.

  2. Compute (f−1)′(1)\bigl(f^{-1}\bigr)'(1)(f−1)′(1).
hints: For (a), show f′f'f′ is positive everywhere; then the monotonicity corollary makes fff strictly increasing, hence one-to-one.
The key estimate is that sin⁡x\sin xsinx never exceeds 111, so 2−sin⁡x2-\sin x2−sinx is bounded below by 111.
For (b) find aaa with f(a)=1f(a)=1f(a)=1 by inspection, then use (f−1)′(1)=1/f′(a)\bigl(f^{-1}\bigr)'(1)=1/f'(a)(f−1)′(1)=1/f′(a).
problems.format: the value of (f⁻¹)′(1)

problems.html: To find the largest area of a rectangle with perimeter 202020, a student sets width xxx, height 10−x10-x10−x, writes A(x)=x(10−x)A(x)=x(10-x)A(x)=x(10−x), finds A′(x)=10−2x=0A'(x)=10-2x=0A′(x)=10−2x=0, so x=5x=5x=5, and then concludes “A′′(x)=−2<0A''(x)=-2<0A′′(x)=−2<0, so this is a minimum.” Identify the error and state the correct conclusion.
hints: Check the student's setup and critical point independently before looking for the error — both are in fact correct.
The mistake is in the classification. Recall what the sign of the second derivative means: negative is concave down.
A concave-down graph at a stationary point is a hill, not a valley. Then compute the area there and note the shape it corresponds to.
problems.format: the correct classification, then the area

problems.html: The equation x3−2x−5=0x^{3}-2x-5=0x3−2x−5=0 has a single real root, which the intermediate value theorem traps in (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) (since f(2)=−1<0f(2)=-1<0f(2)=−1<0 and f(3)=16>0f(3)=16>0f(3)=16>0). Use Newton’s method to pin it down: starting from x0=2x_{0}=2x0​=2, write the iteration explicitly and carry out two steps by hand, tabulating xnx_{n}xn​, f(xn)f(x_{n})f(xn​) and f′(xn)f'(x_{n})f′(xn​) at each stage to obtain x1x_{1}x1​ and x2x_{2}x2​. Comment on how fast the estimate is settling.
hints: Write the iteration down explicitly first: xn+1=xn−f(xn)f′(xn)x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}xn+1​=xn​−f′(xn​)f(xn​)​ with f′(x)=3x2−2f'(x)=3x^2-2f′(x)=3x2−2.
Tabulate f(xn)f(x_n)f(xn​) and f′(xn)f'(x_n)f′(xn​) at each step rather than doing it all in one expression; that is where arithmetic slips creep in.
From x0=2x_0=2x0​=2: f(2)=−1f(2)=-1f(2)=−1 and f′(2)=10f'(2)=10f′(2)=10, so the first correction is a tenth. Carry six decimal places into the second step and compare how many digits have settled.
problems.format: x₁, then x₂ to 6 d.p.

problems.html: For the curve y=1xy=\dfrac1xy=x1​, find the tangent and normal at the point (2,12)(2,\tfrac12)(2,21​), and find where the normal crosses the xxx-axis.
hints: Differentiate 1/x1/x1/x as x−1x^{-1}x−1; the derivative at x=2x=2x=2 gives the tangent's slope.
The normal's slope is the negative reciprocal, so a small tangent slope means a steep normal.
Write the normal in point–slope form, then set y=0y=0y=0 and solve for xxx to find where it crosses the axis.
problems.format: where the normal meets the x-axis

problems.html: Find the equations of the two tangent lines to the parabola y=x2y=x^{2}y=x2 that pass through the point (0,−1)(0,-1)(0,−1).
hints: The point (0,−1)(0,-1)(0,−1) is not on the curve, so you cannot differentiate at it — instead let the point of tangency be unknown.
Call it (a,a2)(a,a^2)(a,a2). The tangent there has slope 2a2a2a and equation y−a2=2a(x−a)y-a^2=2a(x-a)y−a2=2a(x−a).
Now impose the condition that this line passes through (0,−1)(0,-1)(0,−1); you get a quadratic in aaa with two roots, hence two tangent lines.
problems.format: the two tangent slopes, larger first

problems.html: Show that the tangent to y=x3y=x^{3}y=x3 at the point (a,a3)(a,a^{3})(a,a3) (with a≠0a\ne0a=0) meets the curve again at exactly one further point, and that its xxx-coordinate is −2a-2a−2a.
hints: Write down the tangent at (a,a3)(a,a^3)(a,a3) and then set it equal to the curve to find every intersection.
That gives the cubic x3−3a2x+2a3=0x^3-3a^2x+2a^3=0x3−3a2x+2a3=0, and you already know one root: x=ax=ax=a, the point of tangency.
Tangency means x=ax=ax=a is a repeated root, so (x−a)2(x-a)^2(x−a)2 divides the cubic. Divide it out and read off what is left.
problems.format: the x-coordinate of the second meeting point

problems.html: Locate and classify all stationary points of: (a) f(x)=x3−3x2+3x,(b) g(x)=x+1x,(c) h(x)=xe−x.\text{(a)}\ f(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+3x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ g(x)=x+\frac1x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ h(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}.(a) f(x)=x3−3x2+3x,(b) g(x)=x+x1​,(c) h(x)=xe−x.
hints: In (a) the derivative is a perfect square, so it never changes sign — that alone settles the classification without the second-derivative test.
In (b) remember x=0x=0x=0 is outside the domain, so it is not a candidate; solve 1−x−2=01-x^{-2}=01−x−2=0 for the two genuine stationary points.
In (c) factor e−x\mathrm{e}^{-x}e−x out of h′h'h′. Since the exponential is always positive, the sign of h′h'h′ follows the other factor alone.
problems.format: in (b): the local min point; then the local max

problems.html: For f(x)=x4f(x)=x^{4}f(x)=x4, show that f′′(0)=0f''(0)=0f′′(0)=0, so the second-derivative test is inconclusive, and then classify the stationary point at x=0x=0x=0 by another method.
hints: Compute f′f'f′ and f′′f''f′′ and evaluate both at x=0x=0x=0; you will find both vanish.
A vanishing second derivative makes the test inconclusive — it does not mean there is no extremum, only that this method cannot tell.
Fall back on the first-derivative test: check the sign of 4x34x^34x3 on either side of zero. Alternatively, note that x4x^4x4 is never negative.
problems.format: the classification at x = 0

problems.html: Use the closed-interval (extreme-value-theorem) method to find the absolute maximum and minimum of: (a) f(x)=x3−3x on [0,3],(b) g(x)=x4−8x2+3 on [−1,3].\text{(a)}\ f(x)=x^{3}-3x \text{ on } [0,3],\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ g(x)=x^{4}-8x^{2}+3 \text{ on } [-1,3].(a) f(x)=x3−3x on [0,3],(b) g(x)=x4−8x2+3 on [−1,3].
hints: For each, find every critical point first, then discard any that fall outside the given interval.
In (a) the derivative vanishes at x=±1x=\pm1x=±1, but only one of those is in [0,3][0,3][0,3].
Then evaluate fff at the surviving critical points and at both endpoints, and simply pick the largest and smallest values.
problems.format: (a) max, min; then (b) max, min

problems.html: Sketch f(x)=x3−12xf(x)=x^{3}-12xf(x)=x3−12x: give symmetry, intercepts, stationary points and their type, and the concavity.
hints: Check the symmetry first: every power of xxx here is odd, so the curve has rotational symmetry about the origin.
Factorise for the intercepts, then differentiate and solve f′=0f'=0f′=0 for the two stationary points.
The second derivative is linear, so it changes sign exactly once — that single crossing is the inflection point.
problems.format: the local max point; then the local min

problems.html: Sketch f(x)=xx2−1f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^{2}-1}f(x)=x2−1x​: domain, symmetry, intercepts, asymptotes, monotonicity.
hints: Find the domain and the asymptotes first: the denominator factorises, giving two vertical asymptotes.
The function is odd, and as x→±∞x\to\pm\inftyx→±∞ the denominator's higher degree drives the quotient to zero.
Apply the quotient rule. The numerator turns out to be −(x2+1)-(x^2+1)−(x2+1), which is negative for every real xxx — so what does that say about turning points?
problems.format: increasing or decreasing on each branch

problems.html: Sketch f(x)=x−1x+2f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+2}f(x)=x+2x−1​, identifying the asymptotes and the intercepts.
hints: The denominator vanishes at one point, giving a single vertical asymptote.
For the horizontal asymptote, divide top and bottom by xxx: both are degree one, so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients.
The derivative comes out as a positive constant over a square, so the curve is increasing on each branch with no turning points at all.
problems.format: the vertical, then the horizontal asymptote

problems.html: Sketch f(x)=x4−8x2+16f(x)=x^{4}-8x^{2}+16f(x)=x4−8x2+16. (Hint: it factorises.)
hints: Take the hint and factorise: the quartic is a perfect square, which immediately shows it can never be negative.
That also gives the xxx-intercepts, and tells you the curve touches the axis there rather than crossing.
Differentiate and solve f′=0f'=0f′=0; there are three stationary points, and the symmetry means the two outer ones behave identically.
problems.format: the local maximum point

problems.html: A rectangle has its base on the xxx-axis and its two upper corners on the parabola y=12−x2y=12-x^{2}y=12−x2 (with y≥0y\ge0y≥0). Find the dimensions of the rectangle of greatest area, and that area.
hints: Use the symmetry: put the two upper corners at (±x,12−x2)(\pm x, 12-x^2)(±x,12−x2), so the width is 2x2x2x and the height is the parabola's value.
That gives a single-variable area function on the range where the height stays positive.
Differentiate, solve for the stationary point, and confirm with the second derivative — then convert back to the actual dimensions.
problems.format: width, height, then the area

problems.html: A rectangular animal pen of area 600 m2600\,\text{m}^2600m2 is divided into two equal halves by a fence parallel to one pair of sides. Find the dimensions that minimise the total length of fencing used (perimeter plus the internal divider).
hints: Count the fences carefully: the divider runs parallel to one pair of sides, so three fences share that length and two share the other.
Use the fixed area to eliminate one variable, giving the total length as a function of one unknown alone.
Differentiate, set to zero, and check the second derivative is positive. Then read off the other dimension from the area constraint.
problems.format: x, y, then the total fencing in m

problems.html: A closed cylindrical can must hold a volume of 16π cm316\pi\,\text{cm}^{3}16πcm3. Find the radius and height that minimise its total surface area, and verify that at the optimum the height equals the diameter.
hints: Two equations govern the can: the volume constraint and the surface-area expression. Use the first to eliminate the height.
That gives SSS as a function of rrr alone, with a term in r2r^2r2 and a term in 1/r1/r1/r.
Differentiate and solve; the equation reduces to a simple cube. Then compute the height and compare it with the diameter.
problems.format: r, h in cm, then k in S = kπ cm²

problems.html: Find the point(s) on the parabola y=x2y=x^{2}y=x2 closest to (0,32)\bigl(0,\tfrac32\bigr)(0,23​).
hints: Minimise the squared distance rather than the distance itself — the same point minimises both, and the algebra is far cleaner.
With the point on the parabola written as (x,x2)(x,x^2)(x,x2), the squared distance is x2+(x2−32)2x^2+\bigl(x^2-\tfrac32\bigr)^2x2+(x2−23​)2.
Substitute u=x2≥0u=x^2\ge0u=x2≥0 to turn it into a quadratic in uuu; solve, then remember that each positive uuu gives two values of xxx.
problems.format: the two closest points; positive x first

problems.html: A particle moves along a straight line with position s(t)=t3−9t2+24ts(t)=t^{3}-9t^{2}+24ts(t)=t3−9t2+24t metres at time ttt seconds, for 0≤t≤50\le t\le50≤t≤5. Find (a) the times at which it is instantaneously at rest, and (b) its maximum and minimum velocity on the interval.
hints: Velocity is s′s's′; factorise it rather than using the quadratic formula, and the rest times drop out.
For (b) you are extremising the velocity, not the position — so differentiate once more and set v′=0v'=0v′=0.
Then apply the closed-interval method to vvv: compare its values at that interior critical point and at both endpoints of [0,5][0,5][0,5].
problems.format: the rest times; then max and min velocity

problems.html: A “Norman” window is a rectangle topped by a semicircle, the semicircle’s diameter being the top of the rectangle. For a fixed perimeter PPP, find the proportions that maximise the area, and show that at the optimum the rectangle’s height equals the radius of the semicircle.
hints: Write the perimeter in terms of the radius rrr and the rectangle's height hhh — the top of the rectangle is not fenced, since the semicircle sits on it.
Use that to eliminate hhh, giving the area as a function of rrr alone; it is a quadratic in rrr.
Differentiate and solve for rrr, then substitute back to find hhh and compare the two.
problems.format: the k in r = P/(k+π)

problems.html: Evaluate: (a) lim⁡x→0tan⁡x−xx3,(b) lim⁡x→1ln⁡xx−1,(c) lim⁡x→∞x2ex,(d) lim⁡x→0+xx.\text{(a)}\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x-x}{x^{3}},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \lim_{x\to1}\frac{\ln x}{x-1},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^{2}}{\mathrm{e}^{x}},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\ \lim_{x\to0^{+}} x^{x}.(a) x→0lim​x3tanx−x​,(b) x→1lim​x−1lnx​,(c) x→∞lim​exx2​,(d) x→0+lim​xx.
hints: Identify each form before starting: (a) and (b) are 00\tfrac0000​, (c) is ∞∞\tfrac{\infty}{\infty}∞∞​, and (d) is 000^000 and needs rewriting first.
In (c) apply the rule twice — an exponential eventually beats any polynomial.
For (d) write xx=exln⁡xx^{x}=\mathrm{e}^{x\ln x}xx=exlnx; you already know the limit of xln⁡xx\ln xxlnx from the tutorial, and the exponential is continuous.
problems.format: (a)–(d), comma-separated

problems.html: A student writes lim⁡x→0x2+1x+1=Hlim⁡x→02x1=0.\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^{2}+1}{x+1} \overset{\mathrm H}{=}\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0 .x→0lim​x+1x2+1​=Hx→0lim​12x​=0. Explain what is wrong, and give the correct value.
hints: Before applying l'Hôpital, always check that the form really is indeterminate.
Substitute x=0x=0x=0 into the original quotient and see what you get — the numerator and denominator are both perfectly well behaved there.
Since the function is continuous at 000, direct substitution is not merely allowed but is the correct method; the rule was never applicable.
problems.format: the correct value of the limit

problems.html: Show that lim⁡x→∞(1+ax)x=ea\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\Bigl(1+\frac{a}{x}\Bigr)^{x}=\mathrm{e}^{a}x→∞lim​(1+xa​)x=ea for a constant aaa.
hints: The form is 1∞1^{\infty}1∞, which is indeterminate — the base tends to 111 but the exponent grows without bound.
Take logarithms to bring the exponent down: ln⁡y=xln⁡ ⁣(1+ax)\ln y=x\ln\!\bigl(1+\tfrac{a}{x}\bigr)lny=xln(1+xa​), an ∞⋅0\infty\cdot0∞⋅0 form.
Substitute t=1/xt=1/xt=1/x so that t→0+t\to0^{+}t→0+ and the expression becomes ln⁡(1+at)t\dfrac{\ln(1+at)}{t}tln(1+at)​, a clean 00\tfrac0000​. Finish by exponentiating, using continuity.
problems.format: the limit when a = 1, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Show that the equation cos⁡x=x\cos x=xcosx=x has at least one solution in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).
hints: Rearrange into the form 'something =0=0=0' first, so that the intermediate value theorem has a zero to find.
Set f(x)=cos⁡x−xf(x)=\cos x-xf(x)=cosx−x, which is continuous as a difference of continuous functions.
Evaluate at both endpoints; remember the argument of the cosine is in radians, so cos⁡1\cos 1cos1 is not cos⁡1∘\cos 1^{\circ}cos1∘.
problems.format: f(0), f(1) for f = cos x − x, to 2 d.p.

problems.html: Show that x3+x−1=0x^{3}+x-1=0x3+x−1=0 has exactly one real root. (Hint: IVT for existence, the sign of the derivative for uniqueness.)
hints: This is two separate arguments: one for existence, one for uniqueness, and each needs a different tool.
Existence comes from the intermediate value theorem, exactly as in the earlier drill.
Uniqueness comes from the derivative: if f′>0f'>0f′>0 everywhere then fff is strictly increasing, and a strictly increasing function can cross any level at most once.
problems.format: how many real roots the equation has

problems.html: Use the mean value theorem (or the sign of a derivative) to prove that ex≥1+x\mathrm{e}^{x}\ge1+xex≥1+x for all xxx, with equality only at x=0x=0x=0.
hints: Turn the inequality into a statement about a single function: set g(x)=ex−1−xg(x)=\mathrm{e}^{x}-1-xg(x)=ex−1−x and show it is never negative.
Differentiate: g′(x)=ex−1g'(x)=\mathrm{e}^{x}-1g′(x)=ex−1, which is negative to the left of one point and positive to the right.
So ggg decreases and then increases, giving a global minimum. Evaluate ggg there — and note that the equality case is exactly that point.
problems.format: the only x where equality holds

problems.html:
1. For f(x)=x3+2x+1f(x)=x^{3}+2x+1f(x)=x3+2x+1 (one-to-one), find (f−1)′(1)\bigl(f^{-1}\bigr)'(1)(f−1)′(1).

  2. Use the inverse-function theorem to recover  d dxarctan⁡x=11+x2\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\arctan x=\dfrac{1}{1+x^{2}}dxd​arctanx=1+x21​ from tan⁡\tantan.
hints: In (a), find aaa with f(a)=1f(a)=1f(a)=1 by inspection, then use (f−1)′(1)=1/f′(a)\bigl(f^{-1}\bigr)'(1)=1/f'(a)(f−1)′(1)=1/f′(a).
In (b), apply the same rule with f=tan⁡f=\tanf=tan, whose inverse is arctan⁡\arctanarctan, so the derivative is 1/f′(arctan⁡x)1/f'(\arctan x)1/f′(arctanx).
You then need sec⁡2θ=1+tan⁡2θ\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\thetasec2θ=1+tan2θ, and the crucial simplification tan⁡(arctan⁡x)=x\tan(\arctan x)=xtan(arctanx)=x.
problems.format: the value of (f⁻¹)′(1) in part (a)

problems.html: Apply gradient descent to f(x)=(x−3)2f(x)=(x-3)^{2}f(x)=(x−3)2 with η=0.1\eta=0.1η=0.1, starting from x0=0x_{0}=0x0​=0. Write the update rule, compute x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}x1​,x2​,x3​, and identify the limit.
hints: Differentiate first, then substitute into xn+1=xn−ηf′(xn)x_{n+1}=x_n-\eta f'(x_n)xn+1​=xn​−ηf′(xn​) and simplify to a single linear map.
You should reach xn+1=0.8xn+0.6x_{n+1}=0.8x_n+0.6xn+1​=0.8xn​+0.6; now iterate three times from x0=0x_0=0x0​=0.
The limit is the fixed point of that map, which you can find by solving x=0.8x+0.6x=0.8x+0.6x=0.8x+0.6 — and it should agree with where f′f'f′ vanishes.
problems.format: x₁, x₂, x₃, then the limit

problems.html:
For f(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2}f(x)=x2 the gradient-descent update with learning rate η\etaη is xn+1=xn−η (2xn)x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\eta\,(2x_{n})xn+1​=xn​−η(2xn​).

  1. Show that xn=(1−2η)nx0x_{n}=(1-2\eta)^{n}x_{0}xn​=(1−2η)nx0​.

  2. Deduce the exact range of η>0\eta>0η>0 for which xn→0x_{n}\to0xn​→0 for every starting point, and describe the behaviour when η=1\eta=1η=1 and when η>1\eta>1η>1.
hints: Simplify the update: xn+1=xn−2ηxn=(1−2η)xnx_{n+1}=x_n-2\eta x_n=(1-2\eta)x_nxn+1​=xn​−2ηxn​=(1−2η)xn​, a constant multiplier applied over and over.
Repeated multiplication gives a geometric sequence, which is where the formula in (a) comes from.
A geometric sequence tends to zero exactly when the multiplier is smaller than 111 in absolute value. Solve that inequality, and treat the boundary case separately.
problems.format: the k in 0 < η < k for convergence

problems.html:
For each statement, say whether it is true or false and justify briefly.

  1. If f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0 then fff has a local maximum or minimum at ccc.

  2. If f′′(c)=0f''(c)=0f′′(c)=0 then ccc is an inflection point of fff.

  3. A continuous function on an open interval need not attain a maximum value.

  4. If f′(x)>0f'(x)>0f′(x)>0 on an interval, then fff is strictly increasing there.

  5. At a point where f′(a)=0f'(a)=0f′(a)=0, the normal line is horizontal.

  6. l’Hôpital’s rule can be applied to any limit of a quotient.
hints: Four of these are false, and each falls to a single example — x3x^3x3 and x4x^4x4 between them settle the first two.
For (c), the extreme value theorem requires a closed and bounded interval; on an open one the maximum can fail to be attained.
For (e), remember that a horizontal tangent means a vertical normal, not a horizontal one; and (f) is the standing warning about l'Hôpital's rule.
problems.format: (a)–(f): true or false, comma-separated

problems.html: The graph below shows the derivative f′f'f′ of a function fff (not fff itself). Using only this graph, describe fff: state the intervals on which fff is increasing or decreasing, locate and classify its stationary points, and say where fff is concave up or down and where it has a point of inflection.
hints: Everything comes from reading two features off the graph: the sign of f′f'f′, and the slope of f′f'f′.
Where f′f'f′ is above the axis, fff is increasing; where it is below, fff is decreasing. The crossings are therefore the stationary points of fff.
The slope of f′f'f′ is f′′f''f′′, so fff is concave down where the drawn curve is falling and concave up where it is rising — the inflection sits at the vertex of the parabola, not at its roots.
problems.format: where f has its max; its min; its inflection

questions.stem: A student writes lim⁡x→0x2+1x+1=lim⁡x→02x1=0\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0x→0lim​x+1x2+1​=x→0lim​12x​=0, citing l'Hôpital's rule. What has gone wrong?
options: The derivative of x+1x+1x+1 is not 111.
Nothing — the answer 000 is correct.
The quotient rule should have been applied instead of differentiating the two parts.
The form is not indeterminate, so l'Hôpital's rule does not apply at all.
questions.hint: Before reaching for l'Hôpital, substitute x=0x=0x=0 and see what form you actually have.
questions.why: Substituting x=0x=0x=0 gives 0+10+1=1\dfrac{0+1}{0+1}=10+10+1​=1, a perfectly determinate value, so there is nothing for the rule to resolve; applied anyway it produces 000, which is simply wrong. The rule is licensed only for 00\tfrac0000​ and ∞∞\tfrac{\infty}{\infty}∞∞​, and the form must be checked before every application, not just the first. Note that differentiating numerator and denominator separately is what the rule genuinely does — that part was not the error, and it is not the quotient rule.

questions.stem: You find that f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0. Does fff have a local maximum or minimum at ccc?
options: Not necessarily: f(x)=x3f(x)=x^3f(x)=x3 has f′(0)=0f'(0)=0f′(0)=0 but no extremum there.
Yes, provided fff is continuous at ccc.
Yes — that is what an extremum means.
Only if f′′(c)≠0f''(c)\neq0f′′(c)=0 as well.
questions.hint: Try f(x)=x3f(x)=x^3f(x)=x3 at the origin.
questions.why: A vanishing derivative makes ccc a stationary point, which is a candidate rather than a verdict. For x3x^3x3 the derivative vanishes at the origin, yet the function keeps increasing straight through it — a horizontal inflection. To classify you must look further: either check whether f′f'f′ changes sign, or apply the second-derivative test. The last option is close to the truth about that test but is not itself a criterion: f′′(c)≠0f''(c)\neq0f′′(c)=0 does settle the matter, whereas f′′(c)=0f''(c)=0f′′(c)=0 leaves it open rather than ruling an extremum out.

questions.stem: At a stationary point ccc you compute f′′(c)=0f''(c)=0f′′(c)=0. What follows?
options: fff must be constant near ccc.
ccc is a point of inflection.
ccc is neither a maximum nor a minimum.
The second-derivative test says nothing; fall back on the first-derivative test.
questions.hint: Compare x4x^4x4 and x3x^3x3 at the origin. Both have f′′(0)=0f''(0)=0f′′(0)=0 — do they behave the same way there?
questions.why: For f(x)=x4f(x)=x^4f(x)=x4 we have f′′(0)=0f''(0)=0f′′(0)=0 and the origin is a genuine minimum; for f(x)=x3f(x)=x^3f(x)=x3 we have f′′(0)=0f''(0)=0f′′(0)=0 and it is an inflection. The same value of f′′f''f′′ therefore accompanies two different outcomes, which is exactly what 'inconclusive' means — it is not evidence against an extremum. An inflection requires f′′f''f′′ to change sign, not merely to vanish, so the first option is the usual overreach. The first-derivative test still decides both cases in one line.

questions.stem: Why does the extreme value theorem insist on a closed, bounded interval?
options: Because the interval has to contain at least one stationary point.
It does not — the theorem holds on any interval whatsoever.
Because on an open interval a continuous function need not attain a maximum — f(x)=xf(x)=xf(x)=x on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) attains none.
Because derivatives cannot be computed at endpoints.
questions.hint: Try to find the largest value of f(x)=xf(x)=xf(x)=x on the open interval (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).
questions.why: On (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) the values of f(x)=xf(x)=xf(x)=x climb arbitrarily close to 111 without ever reaching it, so there is no largest value; and on (0,1](0,1](0,1] the function 1/x1/x1/x is unbounded. Closedness and boundedness together rule out both failures. This matters practically rather than pedantically: it is what guarantees an optimisation problem has a best answer at all, and that checking the critical points together with the two endpoints exhausts every possibility. Endpoints need no derivative — they are handled by evaluation.

questions.stem: Gradient descent is applied to f(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2}f(x)=x2 with learning rate η=1.5\eta=1.5η=1.5, starting from x0=1x_0=1x0​=1. What happens?
options: It halts immediately, because f′(1)>0f'(1)>0f′(1)>0.
It converges to 000 faster, since each step is larger.
It converges to 000, though more slowly than with a smaller rate.
It diverges: the iterates oscillate with growing amplitude.
questions.hint: Write out the update xn+1=xn−ηf′(xn)x_{n+1}=x_n-\eta f'(x_n)xn+1​=xn​−ηf′(xn​) with η=1.5\eta=1.5η=1.5, and iterate it twice from x0=1x_0=1x0​=1.
questions.why: The update is xn+1=xn−1.5(2xn)=−2xnx_{n+1}=x_n-1.5(2x_n)=-2x_nxn+1​=xn​−1.5(2xn​)=−2xn​, so every step multiplies the distance from the minimum by −2-2−2: the sign alternates while the size doubles. Convergence requires ∣1−2η∣<1|1-2\eta|<1∣1−2η∣<1, that is 0<η<10<\eta<10<η<1; exactly at η=1\eta=1η=1 the iterates flip between ±x0\pm x_0±x0​ forever, and beyond it they blow up. A larger learning rate is therefore not simply a faster one — past the threshold the method stops working altogether.

questions.stem: Newton's method converges far faster than trapping a root with the intermediate value theorem. What does it give up in exchange?
options: It requires a learning rate to be tuned.
The guarantee: a poor starting point, or an xnx_nxn​ where f′(xn)f'(x_n)f′(xn​) is near zero, can derail it.
Nothing — Newton's method is better in every respect.
It requires the function to be a polynomial.
questions.hint: A sign change traps a root, and no later bisection step can lose it. Ask what, if anything, confines Newton's tangent step to that bracket.
questions.why: Once a sign change has been found, the intermediate value theorem has a root trapped and no later step can lose it — slow but certain. Newton instead follows the tangent, roughly doubling the number of correct digits each step, but nothing confines it to the bracket: a bad start can send it towards a different root or away entirely, and a near-zero derivative makes the correction f(xn)/f′(xn)f(x_n)/f'(x_n)f(xn​)/f′(xn​) enormous. It needs no learning rate — that is gradient descent — and it applies to any differentiable function, not only polynomials.

questions.stem: Can the graph of a function cross its own horizontal asymptote?
options: Yes: y=2xx2+1y=\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}+1}y=x2+12x​ has the horizontal asymptote y=0y=0y=0 and meets it at x=0x=0x=0.
No: an asymptote is a line the graph approaches but never meets.
Only for x<0x<0x<0.
Only if the function is discontinuous somewhere.
questions.hint: A horizontal asymptote is a statement about behaviour far out along the axis. Ask whether it constrains anything near the origin.
questions.why: A horizontal asymptote records a limit as x→±∞x\to\pm\inftyx→±∞ — the long-run behaviour — and says nothing whatever about the middle of the graph. Here 2xx2+1→0\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}+1}\to0x2+12x​→0 in both directions, yet the value at x=0x=0x=0 is exactly 000: the graph meets the line, and crosses it, before settling towards it. A vertical asymptote is a different matter, since the function is undefined there and genuinely cannot meet it. Continuity is not the issue either — this example is continuous everywhere. It is worth checking for such crossings when sketching, because they fix which side the curve approaches from.

questions.stem: You are maximising a continuous fff on a closed interval [a,b][a,b][a,b] and find one stationary point ccc inside it. Is f(c)f(c)f(c) the maximum?
options: Yes, provided f′′(c)<0f''(c)<0f′′(c)<0.
Yes: that is what a stationary point is for.
Not necessarily, and the endpoints cannot be checked, because f′f'f′ need not exist there.
Not necessarily: the largest value may sit at aaa or bbb, so the endpoints must be checked too.
questions.hint: The extreme value theorem promises a maximum somewhere on the interval. Write down every place it is allowed to be, then compare values.
questions.why: On a closed, bounded interval a continuous function does attain a maximum, but it may attain it at an endpoint, where there is no reason for the derivative to vanish. So the candidates are the stationary points, any point where f′f'f′ fails to exist, and both endpoints — and the way to finish is to compare fff at all of them, not to trust a derivative test. Take f(x)=2x3−3x2−12x+1f(x)=2x^{3}-3x^{2}-12x+1f(x)=2x3−3x2−12x+1 on [−3,0][-3,0][−3,0]: the interior stationary point x=−1x=-1x=−1 gives 888 and is indeed the maximum, but the minimum is at the endpoint x=−3x=-3x=−3 with f=−44f=-44f=−44, which no derivative test would ever have pointed at. f′′(c)<0f''(c)<0f′′(c)<0 establishes a local maximum only, and a local maximum can still be beaten by an endpoint.

questions.stem: The curve y=x2y=x^{2}y=x2 has tangent slope 444 at x=2x=2x=2. What is the slope of the normal there?
options: −14-\tfrac14−41​
14\tfrac1441​
−4-4−4
444
questions.hint: The normal is perpendicular to the tangent. What do the slopes of two perpendicular lines do to each other?
questions.why: Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1-1−1, so the normal has slope −1m=−14-\dfrac{1}{m}=-\dfrac14−m1​=−41​. Both operations are needed and each distractor performs only one: −4-4−4 takes the sign but not the reciprocal, 14\tfrac1441​ the reciprocal but not the sign, and 444 is the tangent slope over again. The one case to watch is a horizontal tangent, m=0m=0m=0, where the normal is vertical and has no slope at all — there the normal is written x=x0x=x_{0}x=x0​.

questions.stem: f(x)=x3+xf(x)=x^{3}+xf(x)=x3+x is increasing everywhere, and f(1)=2f(1)=2f(1)=2. What is (f−1)′(2)\left(f^{-1}\right)'(2)(f−1)′(2)?
options: 12\tfrac1221​
It cannot be found without a formula for f−1f^{-1}f−1.
14\tfrac1441​
444, the same as f′(1)f'(1)f′(1).
questions.hint: Differentiate f(f−1(x))=xf\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=xf(f−1(x))=x with the chain rule, and read off what the two derivatives are forced to do to each other.
questions.why: Differentiating f(f−1(x))=xf\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=xf(f−1(x))=x gives f′(f−1(x))⋅(f−1)′(x)=1f'\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)\cdot\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=1f′(f−1(x))⋅(f−1)′(x)=1, so (f−1)′(x)=1f′(f−1(x))\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\dfrac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}(f−1)′(x)=f′(f−1(x))1​. At x=2x=2x=2 we are told f−1(2)=1f^{-1}(2)=1f−1(2)=1, and f′(x)=3x2+1f'(x)=3x^{2}+1f′(x)=3x2+1 gives f′(1)=4f'(1)=4f′(1)=4, so the answer is 14\tfrac1441​. The two derivatives are reciprocals rather than equal — which is the reflection in y=xy=xy=x of Unit 1, seen through slopes: a steep graph has a shallow mirror image. No formula for f−1f^{-1}f−1 is needed, and just as well, since this cubic has none worth writing. The value 12\tfrac1221​ would be 1f(1)\dfrac{1}{f(1)}f(1)1​, using the function where the derivative was wanted.
